Kim Philby was a high-ranking officer in British intelligence who was secretly recruited by Soviet intelligence while at Cambridge University. He became the most influential mole in MI6's history, exposing operations and agents throughout the Cold War before defecting to Moscow in nineteen sixty-three.

Born in India, Philby was recruited by Soviet intelligence at Cambridge in the nineteen thirties as part of the Cambridge spy ring while reading for a degree in modernist literature. He rose through the ranks of MI6 to become head of the anti-Soviet counterintelligence section—the perfect position from which to betray agents and operations to Moscow.

Over more than twenty years, Philby provided the KGB with intelligence about British intelligence networks, agent identities, and diplomatic cables, compromising operations across Europe and the Middle East. He helped co-found the intelligence liaison with the CIA after World War II, giving the Soviets access to American intelligence secrets as well. His reports shaped Moscow's entire understanding of Western operations.

When British and American intelligence finally closed in, Philby defected to Moscow in January nineteen sixty-three. He lived comfortably in the Soviet Union until his death in nineteen eighty-eight, writing his memoir in exile. Philby embodied the mole archetype—the trusted insider who exploits intimacy and access to deliver maximum damage.
